title: Apexware - Pricing Sensitivity & Batching Playbook
summary: Intro discovery focused on per-token sensitivity across expected traffic patterns, tradeoffs between latency and unit-cost via batching/caching, and initial scope for a pilot. AE+SE walked through Redwood levers and asked for sample prompts and concurrency to size pilot. Action items and next steps agreed.
action_items: Maya Patel: Send tailored cost model spreadsheet with three batching scenarios (due 2026-08-02)
Liam Chen: Run a short latency benchmark on a representative prompt set (1k synthetic requests) and report p50/p95/p99 (due 2026-08-04)
Marcus Lo: Share production prompt examples and expected concurrency pattern (due 2026-07-31)
next_steps: Redwood to share cost workbook and sample config for batching and KV caching
Schedule 30m pilot scoping meeting w/ engineering (target week of 2026-08-03)
Customer to confirm pilot budget and compliance checklist items
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Jordan Reyes (Apexware Head of ML), Priya Nair (VP Product), Marcus Lo (Infra)

Auto-summary (auto generated, may be rough): Discussed per-token cost sensitivity, batching/caching levers, and pilot scope. Security and residency questions surfaced, and Redwood outlined hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching & KV cache, hosted/dedicated/private, SLAs & fallback, security (KMS, SSO, audit logs)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Liam our SE will jump in on the performance stuff. Jordan, Priya, Marcus thanks for being here. Could we go around real quick on goals for today?
[00:18] Jordan: Yeah sure. Top-line, we want to understand how unit cost changes as we move from hosted to dedicated, and what batching/caching levers we have to hit our 2ms-ish p50 target while keeping burn within our Q4 budget.
[00:32] Priya: And I'll add, we need to map this to a pilot budget — like can we get a 90-day pilot where we validate latency and cost for a subset of traffic.
[00:47] Marcus: Also infra constraints: we need zero inbound data egress for some customer PII workflows, so residency and private deploy options are important.
[00:59] Liam: Great, that's helpful. Quick context on our side — Redwood supports three hosting modes: the hosted API for fast time-to-value, Dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and Private (VPC or on-prem) when residency & strict compliance are required. Each mode has different unit economics and latency profiles.
[01:18] Jordan: Can you quantify the per-token difference between hosted and dedicated? Ballpark.
[01:23] Maya: Ballpark yes — it really depends on model size, sequence length, and batching. For the 7B-ish models you referenced, hosted per-token is typically higher because we bake in multi-tenant overhead and variable capacity costs; Dedicated can be 20-40% lower unit cost at sustained throughput. Private has higher initial platform fee but can lower ops cost if you already own hardware.
[01:43] Priya: That 20-40% swing — is that mostly from being able to batch more aggressively on Dedicated?
[01:50] Liam: Partly. Dedicated gives you consistent GPU residency and predictable KV cache locality, which improves batching efficiency and reduces wasted tokens. There's also quantization and kernel selection differences depending on hardware. But I'd caution that stacking batches increases latency — there's a tradeoff.
[02:08] [02:15] Jordan: Right, our SLO is p50 2s and p95 5s for a conversational assistant. We prioritize p50 but care about p95. If we batch to save, say, 30% token cost, what does that do to p95 typically?
[02:28] Liam: For 7B chat models with short prompts (avg 120 tokens), a moderate batching window (like 20–40ms) may add ~10–30ms to p50, but p95 impact depends on traffic burstiness. If you go to heavy batching windows or queueing we can see larger p95 tails — unless we use smart routing/fallback to low-latency pools.
[02:50] Priya: Smart routing — can you explain?
[02:54] Maya: Sure. We can route requests by policy: latency-first traffic goes to a low-latency pool (maybe Dedicated with reserved capacity), lower-priority traffic goes to a cost-optimized pool. Automatic fallback means if the low-latency pool is saturated, we route to a slightly higher-latency but cheaper variant.
[03:12] Marcus: So for PII-sensitive flows we would want Private or Dedicated? We can't have data leave VPC for those workflows.
[03:19] Liam: Correct. Private (VPC/private) keeps inference inside your network — no egress. Dedicated can be configured with tighter isolation but typically still has some managed control plane traffic — we document data flows. We also support customer-managed KMS and HSM for keys.
[03:33] [03:40] Jordan: On caching — you mentioned KV cache. Our prompts have a lot of repetitive system prompts and persona context. How much savings can we expect from prefix caching?
[03:49] Liam: Prefix/KV cache reduces token compute because repeated prefixes don't need to be re-computed on the attention stack. For heavy repetition you can see 15–40% token compute reduction depending on how much of the prompt is stable. The win is larger when combined with batching because cached prefixes shorten the active sequence length.
[04:08] Priya: Are there pitfalls — e.g., cache staleness or correctness?
[04:12] Liam: You need to manage TTLs and invalidation carefully. We provide tooling to inspect cache hit rates and fall back to full compute when invalid. There's also an evaluation metric we surface: estimated token savings and observed latency changes.
[04:27] [04:34] Marcus: Let's talk pilot sizing — what info do you need from us to size Dedicated vs hosted cost and expected p95?
[04:41] Maya: The key inputs: expected qps/concurrency, average prompt and response lengths (tokens), percent of requests eligible for caching, and acceptance thresholds for latency (p50/p95). If you can share a week of representative traffic or synthetic workload we can model three scenarios: conservative (hosted, small batching), balanced (dedicated with moderate batching and caching), aggressive (private/dedicated heavy batching).
[05:05] Jordan: We can share a sample day and some anonymized prompts. Marcus will pull that.
[05:09] Marcus: Yep I'll get that by Friday.
[05:12] [05:15] Priya: On pricing models — does Redwood do per-token + fixed reserved fees for Dedicated? How does the billing look?
[05:22] Maya: Hosted is straight per-token plus optional features. Dedicated typically has a committed monthly capacity fee plus lower per-token unit price for consumed tokens on that capacity. Private has a platform fee/license and then infra/ops charges. For pilots we can do a short-term reserved capacity or a blended pilot rate.
[05:39] Jordan: If we do a 90-day pilot, can we lock a per-token rate for that window?
[05:45] Maya: Yes, pilots often have a locked pilot rate for the agreed timeframe and usage band; we'll surface that in the pilot proposal.
[05:52] [06:00] Liam: Quick note on quantization — if you can accept lower precision (like 4-bit quant), we can reduce GPU memory and improve batching density which reduces per-token cost. But sometimes you see quality regressions depending on the model and prompt distribution. We recommend evaluating with your prompt set.
[06:19] Priya: Is quantization available on Hosted?
[06:22] Liam: We offer quantized variants in Hosted where supported and in Dedicated you have more control to choose quantized kernels. Private gives you the most control but requires validation.
[06:33] [06:40] Jordan: Security checklist — SOC2, SSO, audit logs, KMS, data residency — do you have docs?
[06:45] Maya: Yes, we have a security pack. We'll share SOC2 attestation, architecture diagrams, SSO/SAML flow docs, and our KMS/HSM integration guide. For residency, we'll show deployment options and what control plane metadata is stored.
[06:58] Priya: Can we get a compliance call with security folks?
[07:01] Maya: Absolutely — we can set that up in parallel to the pilot scoping.
[07:06] [07:15] Marcus: A nit — what about cold-starts and p95 spikes when a model scales up?
[07:20] Liam: We mitigate cold-starts via warm pools and scheduled pre-warming for Dedicated. For Hosted, we maintain hot replicas for common models but there's more variability. We can also use autoscaling policies with conservative thresholds during the pilot to limit p95 spikes.
[07:36] Jordan: Competitor question — other vendors are advertising lower sticker per-token numbers. How do you recommend we compare?
[07:44] Maya: Look at end-to-end effective unit cost: include tail latency penalties, retries, and costs for auxiliary infra (e.g., cache, networking). Also consider developer velocity — Hosted gets you running quickly. We'll provide a cost worksheet that compares apples-to-apples across modes.
[07:58] [08:05] Priya: We need the workbook to show scenarios where batching reduces cost but increases p95 — so product can decide where to place loads.
[08:12] Maya: Noted. We'll include multiple columns: no-batching, moderate-batching, heavy-batching, with expected latency deltas and cost per 1M tokens.
[08:21] Liam: Also include KV cache hit rate sensitivity — a chart that shows unit cost vs cache hit % so you can see break-even points.
[08:31] [08:36] Jordan: For the pilot, what's a realistic minimum commitment for Dedicated?
[08:40] Maya: Typically a month of reserved capacity to get meaningful numbers, but we can do a 90-day pilot with lower commitment structure — depends on volume. For very low volumes, Hosted pilot is easiest.
[08:52] Marcus: Any network egress costs for Dedicated?
[08:55] Liam: If Dedicated is in our managed environment and you have egress out to your cloud, egress applies. Private VPC/on-prem means no egress off your network for inference. We'll map the flows in the security deck.
[09:09] [09:15] Priya: Can you give an example of a cost delta? Like 1M tokens in hosted vs dedicated for our prompt averages?
[09:22] Maya: Without the exact numbers it's fuzzy, but for short convo prompts the hosted might be $X per 1M tokens and Dedicated could be ~25% less in the balanced scenario. We'll commit to exact line numbers in the spreadsheet.
[09:35] Jordan: Ok, let's pivot to operational controls — how do we monitor token burn and set budgets?
[09:42] Liam: Redwood Console has token-level dashboards, route-level cost breakdowns, alerting thresholds, and the ability to throttle or re-route traffic when a budget is hit. We also support token slicing rules — e.g., truncate long responses or use cached summaries to reduce burn.
[09:59] [10:05] Marcus: Do you have an API to pull cost metrics into our internal billing?
[10:09] Maya: Yes, exportable metrics and a usage API. We'll share API docs.
[10:13] Priya: For pilot governance, we'd like a hard budget cap so product can't spike costs accidentally. Possible?
[10:18] Liam: Yes, you can set per-route quotas and global caps. You can also define fallback behaviors — e.g., return cached answer or degrade feature when budget hit.
[10:30] [10:36] Jordan: One more modelling question — do you assume ideal batching in your estimates? Because real traffic is bursty.
[10:43] Liam: Our models allow you to input traffic distribution — if you send us a sample trace we can model realistic batching efficiency vs theoretical maximum. That's why we asked for a representative week.
[10:56] [11:05] Priya: Ok next, timeline — if we sign up for a pilot in early August, what's target delivery and what's needed from Apexware?
[11:13] Maya: Pilot scoping meeting week of Aug 3. We'll need the prompt set, target routes, security requirements, and budget. Redwood will provision pilot capacity (hosted or dedicated), run benchmarks, and give a results deck within 3–4 weeks of start.
[11:28] Jordan: Sounds good. Marcus will confirm the sample prompts by Friday.
[11:33] Marcus: Yep will do.
[11:35] [11:40] Priya: A quick question — do you provide model-change rollback for quality regressions?
[11:44] Liam: Yes, rollout policies support canary and roll-back. We also support A/B tests and automatic fallback to a known-good variant if quality drops. We tie evaluations to prompt sets so we can detect regressions early.
[11:58] [12:05] Jordan: Anything else on legal or procurement we should know?
[12:10] Maya: We have standard enterprise terms, and for pilots we can use a short-term agreement. If you have specific contract language, you'll share it with our legal. We'll also attach the security pack.
[12:22] [12:30] Priya: One last point — our product team will want a simple decision sheet: when to route to low-latency vs cost routes. Can you help co-author that?
[12:38] Maya: Yes, we'll draft a routing decision playbook as part of the pilot deliverables.
[12:44] [12:50] Liam: I'll include suggested batching window sizes and the expected latency impact for your prompt distribution in the modeling.
[12:56] Jordan: Great.
[13:00] Maya: Summarizing next steps — Marcus to share prompts by Friday; Redwood to send cost workbook + security pack and propose pilot scoping slots for week of Aug 3. We'll run a small benchmark and return expected p50/p95 and cost deltas.
[13:18] Priya: That works. Thanks everyone.
[13:22] Marcus: Thanks.
[13:25] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with attachments.

(Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors expected — 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cash' or 'K V cache'; product names can be slightly mis-typed. Filler words and crosstalk present.)
